thread.title_full: 'Redshirt' no longer a word for Clemson or South Carolina football. Here's why - NewsBreak

author: Chapel Fowler
title: 'Redshirt' no longer a word for Clemson or South Carolina football. Here's why - NewsBreak
text:
By Chapel Fowler ,
11 hours ago South Carolina starting quarterback LaNorris Sellers (16) is one of many USC players who had their roster classifications tweaked to remove the word ‘redshirt.’ Jeff Blake/IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Scroll through Clemson and South Carolina’s roster pages, and the word “redshirt” — long associated with college football — is noticeably missing.
Gamecocks quarterback LaNorris Sellers only appeared in three games in 2023 while backing up then-starter Spencer Rattler , but he’s listed as a senior on the 2026 roster instead of a redshirt junior.
Tigers offensive tackle Easton Ware didn’t play a snap last year after a shoulder injury, but he’s listed as a sophomore instead of a redshirt freshman.
Sellers and Ware are among dozens of players on Clemson and USC’s rosters — and among hundreds of players nationally — who got a slight classification refresh in reaction to the NCAA’s new “5 for 5” age-based eligibility model adopted in June.
Previously, college athletes including football players got four years of eligibility, which had to be used in a five-year window. Starting in 2026-27, all Division I athletes now get five years of eligibility within that five-year window.
Although the NCAA’s “5 for 5” system has triggered dozens of lawsuits from former athletes trying to retroactively benefit from the rule change, it’s widely viewed as a positive for athletes still in school and has been praised by coaches.
It’s also led to some university athletics website touch-ups.
‘5 for 5’ rule means no more redshirting The biggest change for college football under 5 for 5? Redshirts no longer exist.
For decades, players had to sit out an entire season to qualify for a redshirt. Since 2018, the NCAA had allowed players to appear in up to four regular-season games and still redshirt. That policy was later expanded to cover conference title games and postseason games and, as of January, nine regular-season games.
Now, though, coaches don’t have to worry about “holding” players to ensure they qualify for a redshirt and get a fifth year of eligibility.
And players don’t have to suddenly leave a team after four games to preserve and extra year of eligibility (which has happened at Clemson and USC in recent years).
A freshman football player could appear in one game, four games, 10 games or 12 games during a season. Regardless of his participation status, he’d still be a sophomore with four years of eligibility left the following season.
It’s a helpful change for players and coaches in all sports but especially football, where injuries and large rosters led to frequent redshirting.
But how does one briefly and accurately display those changes on a roster page?
South Carolina coach Shane Beamer Tracy Glantz/tglantz@thestate.com How Clemson, USC are framing their rosters Clemson and South Carolina are both using the following system to classify players on their rosters, with classes aligning with their current year of eligibility:
Freshman (first year) Sophomore (second year) Junior (third year) Senior (fourth year) Fifth (fifth year) Both schools are following guidance issued by College Sports Communicators (CSC), a national association for sports information directors and others in college sports.
The CSC’s recommendations came after “conversations with communications and creative leaders across the membership, NCAA representatives, members of the compliance community and several media partners,” per a July 27 memo.
The recommendation is for the 2026-27 season only, CSC president Matt Panto wrote.
Under CSC recommendations, a football player’s listed class will always line up with their number of years in the sport (including the current one). If a player is listed as a junior, for example, it means they’re in their third year, regardless of how much they’ve played, if they missed a year with injury or if they’ve transferred.
Although these designations are the same ones used for college grade levels, they don’t refer to academic standing and are exclusively for roster classification.
“We recognize that no single solution perfectly addresses every student-athlete’s individual circumstance under the evolving eligibility landscape,” Panto wrote.
Clemson quarterback Tait Reynolds (2) Stephen Lew/IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect One more change: No more ‘true freshmen’ Although the NCAA’s new system is intended to clean up eligibility questions and generally limit players to five years, there’s still potential for “medical extension waivers” in certain situations, such as a player missing two entire seasons with injury during their five-year eligibility window.
Clemson and USC have players who may meet that criteria, such as Gamecocks receiver Jayden Gibson and Tigers receiver Cole Turner . If those waivers are granted down the line, schools would likely designate such players as sixth-years.
With apologies to exciting first-year players like Clemson’s Tait Reynolds and USC’s J’Zavien Currence , the NCAA’s adoption of “5 for 5” and the elimination of the redshirt system also means the flashy "true freshman” designation will fade.
Why? Well, there’s no longer a “redshirt freshman” to be compared to.
Everyone is a freshman in Year 1 and everyone is a sophomore in Year 2, regardless of whether they started every game or appeared in zero the previous season.
